questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Roman numeral analysis of a stated chord
questions.learningObjective: Identify the Roman numeral for a stated triad in a major key.
questions.stem: Sky log 1: while the mount tracked Orion I worked out a triad of E, G and B in the key of C major and want the numeral for it recorded here.

options.text: The mediant triad, labelled iii, because E is the third scale degree of C major
The tonic triad in first inversion, labelled I6, because E sits at the bottom of the stack
options.misconception: Thinks the third of the chord is the root of the tonic.

options.text: The submediant triad, labelled vi, because A minor shares two of these same pitches
options.misconception: Confuses the mediant with the submediant triad.

options.text: The supertonic seventh, labelled ii7, because a seventh chord is being built on D
options.misconception: Assumes a seventh chord where only a plain triad was given.

questions.explanation: In C major, E is scale degree three, so the triad built on E is the mediant, written iii. It is not the tonic triad because C is the root, and there is no seventh to justify a numeral like ii7.
questions.hint: Name the lowest note of the triad and find its degree.

options.text: Row 1, which has the bass D and the soprano G struck at the same instant
Row 2, which has the soprano sing C and then D in two separate beats
options.misconception: Treats any two notes in a phrase as a harmonic interval.

options.text: Row 3, which has the bass walk down through E, D and C one note at a time
options.misconception: Counts a moving line as though the notes sounded together.

options.text: Row 4, which has the violins play G, then B, then D, one note per beat
options.misconception: Calls a broken chord a harmonic interval.

questions.explanation: A harmonic interval is made when two pitches sound at the same moment, which is what row 1 describes. Rows 2, 3 and 4 all place one pitch after another, which makes them melodic intervals.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Scale degree and its function
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a leading tone differs from a subtonic in scale degree function.
questions.stem: Sky log 4: in C major I noted that the note B sits a half step below the tonic and pulls the ear upward; I want the difference between that note and a subtonic explained here.

answer.exemplar: In major, the seventh scale degree lies a semitone below the tonic and is called the leading tone, because it pulls strongly upward toward the tonic and often forms a dominant triad with a third. In the minor mode, the lowered seventh lies a whole step below the tonic, so it is called the subtonic, lacks that leading pull, and gives a different quality to the close.

questions.explanation: A major key seventh sits a semitone below the tonic and pulls upward, while a lowered seventh sits a whole step below and cannot. The two are the same degree number but different in function.
questions.hint: Ask how far the seventh sits from the tonic.

options.misconception: Ranks the third below the second by letter names alone.

options.text: Major second, then minor third, then perfect fourth, then perfect fifth, in that order
Major second, then perfect fourth, then minor third, then perfect fifth, in that order
options.misconception: Treats the fourth as smaller than the third.

options.text: Perfect fourth, then major second, then minor third, then perfect fifth, in that order
options.misconception: Believes the fourth is the narrowest interval.

questions.explanation: Semitone counts give the order: two for the major second, three for the minor third, five for the fourth and seven for the fifth. Judging by letter names alone puts the third before the second.
questions.hint: Count the semitones of each interval before you sort.

Five semitones, since every fourth spans five semitones however it happens to be spelled

options.text: Seven semitones, since raising the upper note turns the fourth into a perfect fifth
options.misconception: Confuses an augmented fourth with a perfect fifth.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Cadence types and the motion that closes them
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a dominant to tonic close is imperfect when the soprano ends on a third.
questions.stem: Sky log 10: I wrote V then I in C major but the soprano landed on E and my teacher called that an imperfect authentic cadence; I want the reasoning on the record.

answer.exemplar: Both kinds of authentic cadence move from the dominant chord to the tonic chord, so the harmonic motion is identical. The difference lies in the top voice. A perfect authentic cadence ends with the tonic note in the soprano, while an imperfect authentic cadence ends with the third or the fifth of the tonic chord, so the sense of arrival and finality is weaker even though the chords are the same.

questions.explanation: Imperfect and perfect authentic cadences share the same V to I motion; the soprano note is what decides which one has been written.
questions.hint: Look at which chord tone the soprano holds.

options.text: Count every half step from the lower note to the higher, so a fifth of seven semitones is perfect
Count the letter names inclusively and ignore the accidentals, so a fifth is always five semitones
options.misconception: Counts letter names and ignores accidentals entirely.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Counting semitones across a flat note
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a flat on the upper note changes the semitone count.
questions.stem: Sky log 16: the passage from G up to B flat gave me trouble because the flat shifts a note I know well; explain what the accidental does to the count and to the interval name.

answer.exemplar: In its natural form, G up to B is a major third of four semitones, because the two notes are two whole steps apart. Lowering the upper note with a flat pulls it down by one semitone, so the span becomes three semitones while the letter names still spell a third. A third of three semitones is a minor third, so the flat simply produces the minor form of the interval.

questions.explanation: Flattening the upper note removes one semitone from the span, so four becomes three and the interval narrows from major to minor.
questions.hint: Ask what the count would be without the flat.

questions.stem: Sky log 19: someone asked me why the same two pitches can make two different kinds of interval; which statement gives the true reason?

A harmonic interval is always larger than the melodic interval built from the same notes
options.misconception: Assumes the size decides the harmonic or melodic label.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Counting semitones in an augmented fourth
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a pair of notes is an augmented fourth rather than a perfect fourth.
questions.stem: Sky log 22: F up to B sounds uneasy to me and I want the written reasoning in the log; explain why that pair is an augmented fourth and not a perfect fourth.

answer.exemplar: The letters F and B span four scale positions, so the interval must be some kind of fourth. A perfect fourth measures five semitones, and raising the upper note of a perfect fourth by one chromatic step widens the interval to six semitones, which is the definition of an augmented fourth. Because six semitones also fills half of an octave, the pair sounds tense and leans outward in resolution.

questions.explanation: A fourth spanning six semitones rather than five has been widened by one chromatic step, and that widening is exactly what the word augmented means.
questions.hint: Start from a perfect fourth and widen it.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Scale degree and its function
questions.learningObjective: Explain how scale degrees divide into tonic, dominant and subdominant function.
questions.stem: Sky log 28: I want the function of each scale degree written out plainly in the log, because I keep confusing the two middle degrees; explain the three functional areas.

answer.exemplar: In a major key the scale degrees fall into three functional areas. The tonic area is built from degrees one, three and six, so chords there feel settled and can stand in for the tonic. The dominant area is built from degrees five and seven, and the subdominant area from degrees two and four, so a chord on either of those degrees prepares the phrase for a move toward the dominant.

questions.explanation: Degrees five and seven belong to the dominant area because they want to push toward the tonic, while degrees two and four belong to the subdominant area and want to move on toward the dominant.
questions.hint: Ask which area each degree pushes the music toward.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Cadence types and the motion that closes them
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an authentic close from a plagal close by the chord motion.
questions.stem: Sky log 34: I want the difference between a plagal close and an authentic close written into the log, because my teacher corrected me on it; explain what ends each phrase.

answer.exemplar: An authentic cadence ends a phrase by motion from the dominant chord to the tonic chord, so the ear hears the goal actually arriving. A plagal cadence ends by motion from the subdominant chord to the tonic chord, usually the bass falling a fourth or rising a fifth, and it sounds like a gentle confirmation rather than an arrival. Both can close a phrase, but only the authentic cadence carries the tension of the dominant being resolved.

questions.explanation: An authentic cadence resolves the dominant to the tonic, while a plagal cadence moves the subdominant to the tonic, so the two close a phrase with quite different kinds of motion.
questions.hint: Ask which chord moves to the tonic in each case.

questions.topic: Counting semitones across a flat note
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a flat on the upper note narrows an interval.
questions.stem: Sky log 40: I want the log to explain why a flat on the upper note shrinks an interval instead of widening it; put that reasoning into plain words.

answer.exemplar: A flat lowers a pitch by one semitone, so when it appears on the upper note of an interval it pulls that note down toward the lower one and the distance between them shrinks. The letter names, and therefore the interval number, stay exactly the same. That is why G up to B flat is a minor third of three semitones while G up to B is a major third of four, even though both pairs span the same three letters.

questions.explanation: Lowering the top note reduces the distance between the two pitches while the letter span and the interval number stay fixed.
questions.hint: Ask which note the accidental moves.

options.text: Nine semitones, since the letter span of four steps must be counted twice
options.misconception: Doubles the letter span when counting the fourth.

questions.explanation: A perfect fourth holds five semitones and sharpening the upper note widens it to six, which is what an augmented fourth is. The letter span stays a fourth because the note names are unchanged.
questions.hint: Add one chromatic step to the five of a fourth.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Counting semitones in a minor third
questions.learningObjective: State what makes an interval minor rather than major.
questions.stem: Sky log 55: the class asked what turns a third into a minor third instead of a major third; which statement is true?

options.text: The same letter span but one fewer semitone, so three instead of four for a third
One more letter name in the span, so the third becomes a fourth
options.misconception: Confuses the letter count with the semitone count.

options.text: The same semitone count but one fewer letter name in the span
options.misconception: Swaps which factor determines the quality.

options.text: An accidental on the lower note only, since the upper note stays fixed
options.misconception: Believes only the lower note can change the quality.

questions.explanation: Major and minor share the letter span and differ only in semitone count, so a third of four semitones is major and three is minor. Changing the letter names would change the number instead.
questions.hint: Keep the letter span fixed and compare the counts.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Counting semitones across a flat note
questions.learningObjective: Count the semitones spanned by a given flattened upper note.
questions.stem: Sky log 56: the pair B flat up to D flat sits in my flat-side exercise on the submediant chord, and I recorded the semitone span between the two notes.
questions.explanation: B flat up to D flat spans three semitones, a minor third. Each note is a semitone below its natural partner, so lowering both leaves the width of the interval unchanged.
questions.hint: Compare it with the span from B flat up to D natural.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Roman numeral analysis of a stated chord
questions.learningObjective: Identify the correct Roman numeral and inversion for a chord in a chart.
questions.stem: Sky log 57: my chart lists chords of C major with their inversions; only one row is labelled correctly, so which row is it?

options.text: Row 1, which puts G in the bass and labels the chord iii6
Row 2, which puts C in the bass and labels the chord I64
options.misconception: Confuses second inversion with root position.

options.text: Row 3, which puts B in the bass and labels the chord V64
options.misconception: Calls first inversion a second inversion.

options.text: Row 4, which puts C in the bass and labels the chord IV2
options.misconception: Invented a third inversion for a plain triad.

questions.explanation: E minor with G in the bass is first inversion, so it is written iii6. The other rows misread the bass note, and a triad such as F major cannot take a third inversion figure at all.
questions.hint: Check the bass note before the figure in each row.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Cadence types and the motion that closes them
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a phrase can close without ever reaching the tonic.
questions.stem: Sky log 58: I want a note in the log on why a phrase can sound finished without ever reaching the tonic, and on what that close is called; explain.

answer.exemplar: A half cadence ends a phrase on the dominant chord, so the music sounds unsettled rather than arrived at, and the listener expects more to follow. It is often used at the end of a first section, leaving the tonic for later. A deceptive cadence does reach a final chord, but the dominant moves to the submediant instead of the tonic, so the expected arrival is evaded.

questions.explanation: A half cadence stops on the dominant so the phrase leaves the tonic unresolved, while a deceptive cadence evades the tonic by sending the dominant to the submediant instead.
questions.hint: Ask whether the tonic chord ever sounds at the close.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Harmonic against melodic interval
questions.learningObjective: Order harmonic and melodic events by the size of the interval involved.
questions.stem: Sky log 59: four events from tonight's practice are A4 and E4 struck together, C4 to D4 sung in one breath, F4 and A4 struck together, and B4 to C5 sung in one breath; sort them smallest first.

options.text: B to C, then C to D, then F and A, then A and E, from smallest to largest
C to D, then B to C, then F and A, then A and E, from smallest to largest
options.misconception: Ranks the whole step below the half step.

options.text: B to C, then C to D, then A and E, then F and A, from smallest to largest
options.misconception: Swaps the two simultaneous fourths and fifths.

options.text: F and A, then B to C, then C to D, then A and E, from smallest to largest
options.misconception: Starts with a simultaneous interval, not the smallest step.

questions.explanation: The counts are one semitone for B to C, two for C to D, four for F and A and five for A and E, so that is the order. Judging by letter names would move the whole step ahead of the half step.
questions.hint: Count the semitones of each event before sorting.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Scale degree and its function
questions.learningObjective: Trace a function chart to the degree that builds the dominant triad.
questions.stem: Sky log 60: my function chart runs: line 1 put degree one in the tonic area, line 2 put degree five in the dominant area, line 3 put degree seven with the dominant, line 4 put degree four in the subdominant area.

options.text: Degree five, because the dominant triad is built on the fifth scale degree of the key
Degree four, because the dominant triad is built a fourth above the tonic
options.misconception: Builds the dominant from the fourth degree.

options.text: Degree seven, because the leading tone must be the root of the dominant
options.misconception: Makes the leading tone the root of the dominant chord.

options.text: Degree two, because the supertonic triad sits a fifth below the dominant
options.misconception: Confuses the supertonic with the dominant degree.

questions.explanation: The dominant triad is the triad on scale degree five, so degree five builds it. Degree four belongs to the subdominant area and degree two to the subdominant as well, so neither can be right.
questions.hint: The dominant triad comes from the degree that names the key.
